author: Mark Dundas
bottom_line: Multiple rider-triggered avalanches on a buried weak layer keep the Persistent Slab as today's primary concern. If more sunshine than forecast arrives, expect a wet avalanche problem to develop in the abundant, cold, dry surface snow.  Choose low-angle slopes sheltered from the sun and wind for a safer experience.
hazard_discussion:
Saturday's sunny skies and deep, cold, unconsolidated snow drew many people out to enjoy the backcountry. Riders experienced superb snow conditions in sheltered terrain, with wind-affected snow on wind-exposed slopes. We received a whopping dozen public observations from all zones! Thank you so much for helping us out.

Josh and I visited the southern Whitefish Range on Friday to take a closer look at a large avalanche remotely triggered by a rider. This slide failed on a buried weak layer 2 feet below the surface. We also noted a fresh but smaller slide on this same layer, triggered by a snowbiker. You can read the observation here. 

Wet Loose: Today's wild card is the amount of sun we will receive. There is a lot of dry, cold snow available to become wet and develop wet loose problems. If today's forecast of partly to mostly cloudy conditions becomes mostly sunny, wet loose activity will become the primary problem across all three zones. 

Wind Slab: Wind continues to blow and transport snow in all zones. However, we believe this problem is isolated in the Whitefish Range and Swan Range, where less snow has fallen, and we have removed this from today's problem list. We have removed the wind slab problem from these zones, but you should continue to evaluate leeward slopes that show fresh evidence of wind-affected snow. 

Unfortunately, a large avalanche resulted in the deaths of two riders in the Washington Cascades. You can read more about that here.

forecast_avalanche_problems.discussion:
Triggering a 1-3 foot thick slab avalanche on a buried weak layer remains possible. Three rider-triggered slides occurred on this layer in the Whitefish Range over the past few days. 

The conditions for a Persistent Slab avalanche are not present on all slopes, and it's challenging to determine where they are or aren't. The safest bet is to assume that the troublesome slab/weak-layer/crust combination exists on all slopes. You may or may not experience obvious signs of instability—snowpack collapsing or cracks shooting out from your skis or sled—before triggering an avalanche. The resulting slides may propagate farther than expected, triggering a large avalanche.

Friday's avalanche was triggered remotely from the side of a steep slope. This could also occur from lower-angle terrain above or below a steep slope.

Reduce your chances of triggering one of these beasts by selecting low-angle slopes not connected to steeper terrain.

forecast_avalanche_problems.name: Persistent Slab
forecast_avalanche_problems.problem_description: Persistent Slab avalanches are the release of a cohesive layer of snow (a slab) in the middle to upper snowpack, when the bond to an underlying persistent weak layer breaks. Persistent layers include: surface hoar, depth hoar, near-surface facets, or faceted snow. Persistent weak layers can continue to produce avalanches for days, weeks or even months, making them especially dangerous and tricky. As additional snow and wind events build a thicker slab on top of the persistent weak layer, this avalanche problem may develop into a Deep Persistent Slab.

forecast_avalanche_problems.discussion:
Cold, dry snow is widespread in the mountains, and any slope that sees direct sun today may produce loose avalanches as surface snow warms (dry or wet). Cloud cover is the wild card and will determine where this problem occurs. Meanwhile, southwest- and west-facing slopes may have already seen some melting from Saturday afternoon’s sunshine, while east-facing slopes could be seeing their first exposure to sunlight this morning. 

Managing this problem is fairly straightforward. If the sun is shining on the slope you are on—or on slopes above you—expect the potential for snow to start shedding and move to lower-angle terrain, switch aspects, or step into the shade. Snow falling from trees, rollerballs, pinwheels, and a soggy surface snow are good signs that loose avalanche problems may be developing. Keep in mind that snow on rock bands, cliffy features, and high above you can warm and release before the snow at your feet does. Even small wet loose avalanches can entrain significant snow and have serious consequences if they knock you off balance or push you into terrain traps.

forecast_avalanche_problems.name: Wet Loose
forecast_avalanche_problems.problem_description: Wet Loose avalanches are the release of wet unconsolidated snow or slush. These avalanches typically occur within layers of wet snow near the surface of the snowpack, but they may quickly gouge into lower snowpack layers. Like Loose Dry Avalanches, they start at a point and entrain snow as they move downhill, forming a fan-shaped avalanche. Other names for loose-wet avalanches include point-release avalanches or sluffs. Loose Wet avalanches can trigger slab avalanches that break into deeper snow layers.
